title: Nusseibeh makes her case for the UN top job
summary: Lana Nusseibeh, a late entrant to succeed Antonio Guterres, says she would serve independently and put Sudan's war first. Supporters see a seasoned diplomat who can still reshape a deadlocked race.
body:
Lana Nusseibeh has entered the contest to become the next United Nations secretary general with a clear pitch: she would answer to the Charter, not to Abu Dhabi, and she would be judged by what she delivers in her first hundred days.

The 48 year old state minister of the United Arab Emirates and former ambassador in New York is a late arrival in a race that must settle before Antonio Guterres leaves at year end. She said every candidate comes from somewhere, that great and small states alike have faced UN findings on international humanitarian law, and that she would speak frankly to every government while balancing pragmatism and principle. Sudan's war and its humanitarian catastrophe would be her immediate priority.

Critics, including Sudan's military authorities, some rights groups and former Human Rights Watch director Kenneth Roth, argue she is unfit because she rebutted claims that the UAE backed the Rapid Support Forces while serving as a diplomat. Abu Dhabi denies arming that force. Her answer is to invite scrutiny of her record once in office rather than of the capital she once represented.

Supporters see a different ledger. She comes from a Palestinian family with roots in Jerusalem; her father Zaki worked as a translator to Sheikh Zayed. The Palestinian Authority and several Gulf governments have endorsed her. Diplomats who watched her in New York recall adroit floor work, and she has backed Gaza humanitarian efforts. On the Board of Peace linked to the Trump Gaza plan she frames the body as complementary to the UN and useful where the system is gridlocked.

Her vision is to restore peacemaking so the UN sits at the centre of crises rather than as a spectator. She favours sharper priorities over blunt cuts, and closer partnership with the private sector, the World Bank, the IMF and regional development banks. Criticism from President Donald Trump, she suggests, is galvanising a push for efficiency, though she has not spoken to him about her candidacy.

The politics remain open. Tradition points to a Latin American turn, with figures including Costa Rica's Rebeca Grynspan and Argentina's Rafael Grossi in the field, while Turkey's Volkan Sinirlioglu has entered. Washington has played down regional rotation. An unofficial Security Council straw poll put Nusseibeh fourth, with another round due later Thursday. Frontrunners face resistance among the permanent five, which is why her late bid retains room to grow.

title: Vance breaks ranks, ties Republican losses to the Iran war
summary: Vice President JD Vance has given an unusually blunt account of why his party lost ground in the midterms, pointing to the conflict with Iran. The comments stand out as one of the sharpest public departures from a sitting president by his own deputy in years.
body:
Vice President JD Vance has publicly pinned his party's midterm defeat on the war with Iran, in a statement that quickly became one of the starkest open breaks between a sitting president and his deputy in recent American politics.

Writing on X after Democrats took both chambers of Congress, Vance said the conflict was the clear reason former Trump voters walked away. He challenged anyone who still defended the war to say plainly that losing the Senate for years was a price worth paying. President Donald Trump, who had already conceded that the war weighed on the result, largely accepted the framing while insisting he would make the same choice again to stop Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.

Washington insiders have long known that Vance backed the campaign in public while raising doubts in private. Those doubts stayed off the record until this week. His post carefully avoided naming Trump, leaned on unnamed pollsters for the diagnosis, and ended with a four point recovery plan: end the war, focus on living costs and inflation, put America first, and change the relationship with Israel. That list reads like an early stump speech for a possible 2028 run, even though he has not declared.

Republican strategists say the vice president is testing how far he can mark distance without losing the president's blessing. Trump has prized loyalty but has so far treated Vance's critique lightly, and has still not said who he would back as a successor. The midterms are only days old. Whether the statement was a one off vent or the opening move of a post Trump contest will become clearer as the party debates what went wrong.

title: Republicans weigh a new direction as Vance looks to 2028
summary: After heavy midterm losses, senior Republicans are debating how far to move away from the Trump brand. Vance is seen positioning himself for a fresh start ahead of the next presidential race.
body:
Senior Republicans are scrambling for a new course after Democrats swept both houses of Congress in this week's midterms, and much of the debate turns on how far the party can step back from President Donald Trump's brand without tearing itself apart.

Vice President JD Vance moved first. Hours after the scale of the defeat became clear, he argued on X that the war with Iran, and the strain of American ties to Israel, had driven former Trump voters to the other side. He told critics who had warned the party that they were right, and urged them to channel that energy into choosing Republicans who share their worldview. Oil markets reacted in kind: Brent crude slipped as traders judged that a weaker White House hand made a fresh round of strikes less likely.

The economic backdrop is harsh. After Tehran closed the Strait of Hormuz early in the conflict, crude surged and has stayed elevated for months, feeding higher fuel and food prices at home. Analysts say any serious 2028 contender will have to show daylight from the most unpopular parts of Trump's record, above all the war. Vance has publicly supported the campaign while privately pressing for an end to it, and last week he wrote to Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei proposing talks. Trump, by contrast, has said the war ends when he decides.

Early primary sounding puts Vance well ahead of Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Donald Trump Jr. Texas senator Ted Cruz called the result a blue tsunami and blamed high prices, tariffs and a war that dragged on. Florida governor Ron DeSantis warned that losing Texas as an anchor would leave the party nationally unviable. The field is still open. The hard question is whether anyone can keep the MAGA base while winning back voters who have drifted away.

title: Netanyahu claims fraud over Arab turnout in Israeli vote
summary: Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies say Arab voters unfairly decided last month's election. Electoral officials confirm some irregularities are under investigation but insist they could not have changed the outcome.
body:
Benjamin Netanyahu and allies in his camp say Arab voters wrongly decided last month's Israeli election, casting the result as tainted. The claim has hardened into a political message as the former prime minister contests his defeat and tries to keep his coalition together.

Electoral officials acknowledge that some irregularities are under investigation. They also say those issues could not have altered the overall outcome. That official line undercuts the fraud narrative even as it keeps limited probes alive, leaving room for both legal process and continued political argument.

Arab turnout and voting patterns have long been a sensitive theme in Israeli campaigns. This time the defeated camp has elevated the issue into an attack on the legitimacy of the count itself. Supporters of the new majority reject that framing and point to the election authority's assessment that the result stands.

The dispute matters beyond party talking points. It shapes how quickly a new government can settle, how opposition politics organise, and how outside partners read Israel's domestic stability. For now the formal position of the electoral authorities is clear: probes continue where warranted, but they do not rewrite who won.

title: Mojtaba Khamenei's quiet style hints at a new way of ruling Iran
summary: Iran's new supreme leader appears to be consulting widely rather than issuing orders from the top. Analysts ask whether this emerging approach could open a path towards peace.
body:
Iran's new supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, is governing without public speeches or released audio. Since succeeding his father in March he has worked through written decrees and a sequence of reported meetings with senior officials, a style shaped in part by security advice after he was injured in the February strike that killed Ali Khamenei.

Early meetings in May and August mainly reassured Iranians that the new leader was alive and active. A tighter cluster of four meetings in October, spanning parliament, the judiciary, the national security apparatus and the military, looks more like a decision system coming online. Those talks followed appointments that replaced commanders killed in the war, including a new armed forces chief of staff and a new Revolutionary Guard commander, and the elevation of Mohsen Rezaei as secretary of the Supreme National Security Council.

The timing tracks external mediation. After Pakistani, Qatari, Saudi and Turkish envoys shuttled compromise ideas to Tehran, meetings with Iran's chief negotiator and with Rezaei were announced in quick succession. Messages from those sessions run in parallel: conditions for ending a draining state of neither war nor peace, and orders for immediate retaliation if attacks resume. Washington still wants nuclear concessions before talks restart; Tehran wants the naval blockade eased, frozen assets freed and oil exports restored.

Comparisons with the long consultations before the 2015 nuclear deal are tempting but imperfect. Then the process stretched over years under sanctions. Now the window is compressed amid open conflict. The machinery of consultation appears to be working. Whether it can deliver a settlement as consequential as 2015, while the leader himself stays unseen, remains the open question in Tehran.

title: Melania Trump emerges as an unlikely broker on Ukraine
summary: Officials in both Moscow and Kyiv credit the first lady's team with pushing through the evacuation of a besieged town. Both capitals also saw value in handing her a humanitarian success.
body:
Melania Trump has unexpectedly become a named figure in Ukraine diplomacy after officials in Moscow and Kyiv credited her team with driving an evacuation from a besieged town. The first lady is not a formal envoy, yet both sides describe her circle as the force that pushed the humanitarian move across the line.

The episode sits at the junction of politics and optics. For Kyiv, a successful evacuation under American first lady sponsorship is a tangible relief for civilians and a signal that channels beyond the usual military brief still work. For Moscow, granting the same win costs little militarily while offering a rare positive note with Washington's household at a moment when the wider war remains grinding.

Neither capital presents the evacuation as a ceasefire. It is framed as a narrow humanitarian carve out. Even so, the fact that both governments chose to highlight her role suggests each saw value in giving her a visible success. That may open a thin lane for further people centred steps, or it may remain a one off.

What is clear is that the first lady's staff are now part of the public story of the conflict's civilian track. Whether that influence grows will depend on whether similar operations follow, and on how closely the White House ties them to any broader talks.

title: Hoax bomb threats rattle European air travel again
summary: More than a dozen flights targeted on Thursday touched down without incident, following a similar wave earlier in the week. The false alarms are adding to nerves over the region's airspace.
body:
A fresh wave of hoax bomb threats hit European air travel on Thursday, with more than a dozen flights named as targets before all of them landed safely. The false alarms follow a similar burst earlier in the week and have deepened anxiety across the region's airspace.

Airlines and security agencies treated the warnings as real until cleared, which means diversions, delays and heavy screening even when nothing dangerous is found. That pattern is costly for carriers and exhausting for passengers, and it stretches already busy airport police and crew.

Officials have not publicly pinned the campaign on a single group. What matters operationally is that the threats are numerous enough to keep crews on alert and to force repeated disruption without an actual device. Hoax calls of this kind are a known tactic: low cost for the perpetrator, high cost for the system.

Travellers should expect continued caution. Authorities say the flights involved on Thursday ended without incident, but the earlier wave shows the problem is not a one day spike. Until the source is shut down, European aviation will keep absorbing the friction of alerts that prove empty after the fact.

title: Milei aide reportedly met Bolsonaro as he fled Brazil
summary: A senior adviser to Argentina's president greeted defeated candidate Flavio Bolsonaro at an Argentine airport, according to people involved. The episode raises fresh questions about Buenos Aires' role in his departure.
body:
A senior adviser to Argentina's president Javier Milei reportedly met Flavio Bolsonaro at an Argentine airport as the defeated Brazilian presidential candidate left Brazil, according to people involved in the episode. The account places Buenos Aires closer to the departure than a purely passive neighbour.

Flavio Bolsonaro's exit after a lost election was already politically charged at home. The reported airport greeting by a Milei aide sharpens questions about how much help, if any, Argentine officials gave and whether it was personal, informal or coordinated. Those involved have described a meeting on arrival; they have not framed it as a formal asylum process in public summaries available so far.

The story matters for regional politics. Brazil and Argentina are major neighbours whose leaders often trade barbs across the border. Any perception that Argentine power circles eased a Brazilian rival's flight will feed opposition attacks in Brasilia and awkward questions in Buenos Aires.

For now the public record rests on those accounts of an airport meeting. Investigators and journalists will press for passenger logs, messages and official statements. Until those appear, the core fact on offer is limited but pointed: a Milei adviser was there when Bolsonaro arrived.

title: Joshua Wong handed ten years in prison in Hong Kong
summary: The activist who became the face of the city's democracy movement has been sentenced under the national security law. He is one of hundreds held under the sweeping legislation.
body:
Joshua Wong, long the most recognisable face of Hong Kong's democracy protests, has been sentenced to ten years in prison for colluding with foreign forces under the city's national security law. He is already serving time for subversion and had been due for release in January; only a small slice of the new term will run alongside the old one, so he faces another decade behind bars.

Wong, who turned 30 last month, pleaded guilty in September. Prosecutors said that in mid to late 2020 he worked with other campaigners, including self exiled activist Nathan Law, to seek foreign sanctions against Beijing. Hong Kong's chief executive John Lee called Wong and Law primary culprits in harming the city's stability. Beijing's foreign ministry backed the ruling as lawful defence of national security.

The sentence drew sharp responses abroad. The UK called it an example of the law being used against political expression and urged an end to unjust prosecutions under it. The US consulate said Beijing was going to extraordinary lengths to silence advocates of basic freedoms. Human Rights Watch labelled the term cruel and unjust, arguing that stacking charges keeps society subdued while limiting international outcry.

Wong's activism began in his teens with Scholarism and the Umbrella Movement, and later Demosisto with Law and Agnes Chow. Hundreds have been detained under the 2020 security law. The heaviest term so far went to media tycoon Jimmy Lai, jailed for twenty years on a related collusion conviction. Wong nodded to supporters in a packed gallery as the judge read the reasons, then returned to a prison path that now stretches deep into the 2030s.

title: France hit by fresh strikes as unions press for answers
summary: Five major unions joined a national day of walkouts and marches over wages and rising costs. Hundreds of protests were planned across the country.
body:
France faced a fresh national day of strikes and marches on Thursday as five major unions joined students and cost of living protesters in a coordinated push for higher pay and clearer answers from the government. Union leaders said more than 250,000 people were already on the streets in dozens of towns by early afternoon, calling that only the start.

Disruption hit schools, hospitals and transport. The Eiffel Tower and some Louvre galleries closed. Refinery workers were urged to halt production, and the country was expected to import more electricity than it generated because of nuclear plant stoppages. Unions want a higher minimum wage and a net pay rise of about 100 euros a month. The education ministry put teacher strike participation at 16 percent, while unions said more than a quarter of lycées and most universities were affected.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez deployed around 70,000 police and promised a firm response to violence. Clashes broke out in Lyon, where a car was set alight near the Rhone, and in Rennes, where masked groups confronted officers. Thursday's Paris march was allowed through the centre but not on the unions' preferred route past the National Assembly and the Elysee.

The wave began in September over conditions in high schools and has widened to workers and a revived yellow vest current that plans further blockades into the weekend. Ministers have tried to blunt anger by releasing diesel from strategic stocks and promising to overhaul the Parcoursup university admissions system by 2028. Union leaders say that is not enough while prices stay high and public services feel stretched.

title: British Ebola patient flown home from Congo
summary: A UK healthcare worker infected in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is being brought back for specialist care and is said to be stable. Officials say the risk to the public remains low as the outbreak has claimed more than 5,000 lives across Africa.
body:
A British healthcare worker infected with Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is being brought home for specialist treatment and is described as stable. UK officials say the risk to the wider public remains low even as the current African outbreak has killed more than 5,000 people across the continent.

Evacuating an infected citizen to a high containment unit is standard practice for countries with that capacity. It allows intensive care under controlled conditions and removes pressure from local clinics already coping with a large epidemic. Public health teams will monitor close contacts from the journey and from any earlier exposure, which is why officials stress that community risk at home stays limited when protocols are followed.

The scale of the outbreak abroad is the graver story. Thousands of deaths signal a virus that is still finding victims faster than containment can close every chain. International medical staff remain essential on the ground, which is how this British worker became a patient rather than only a caregiver.

For Britain the immediate task is clinical: get the patient into the right facility, protect crews and contacts, and keep the public informed without alarm. For the wider response the priority remains the same as before this case: break transmission where the epidemic is burning, and support the health systems carrying the heaviest load.

title: Six killed in New York building fire
summary: A blaze in a New York City building has left six people dead and others hurt. Around 230 firefighters and medics responded, and the cause is still being investigated.
body:
Six people have died in a major fire at a residential building in Brooklyn, New York City, officials say, with several others hurt. The blaze was reported around 01:40 local time on Thursday, which is 06:40 GMT, and more than 230 firefighters and emergency medics were sent to the scene near Sunset Park.

Crews found the first and second floors already engulfed when they arrived. Four people were pronounced dead at the scene. A man and a woman later died in hospital. Six other civilians were injured, two of them critically, and three firefighters were also hurt. Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he was heartbroken by the deaths and asked New Yorkers to pray for those still recovering.

The cause remains under investigation. A hazardous materials team attended because a lithium ion battery was present, though officials have not said whether it started the fire. That detail will matter for any later safety advice, but investigators have not yet linked it to the ignition.

For now the focus is on the victims, the injured and the families. Fire officials will piece together how the flames moved so quickly through the lower floors, and whether alarms, exits or building systems played any part. Until that work is done, the public facts are the death toll, the scale of the response, and an open inquiry.

title: Finland jails two sailors over Baltic cable damage
summary: A Finnish court found the captain and boatswain of a cargo ship guilty of aggravated criminal damage to an undersea cable. The incident happened in the Gulf of Finland last year.
body:
A Finnish court has sentenced the captain and boatswain of a cargo ship to prison for aggravated criminal damage after an undersea cable was harmed in the Gulf of Finland last year. The ruling turns a long running infrastructure scare in the Baltic into a concrete criminal outcome against two crew members.

Damage to undersea cables has worried northern European governments because those lines carry power and data between states that sit on Russia's doorstep. Investigators have looked hard at whether incidents were accidents, negligence or deliberate acts. In this case the court found the two sailors guilty of aggravated criminal damage, a serious charge that goes beyond a simple navigation mishap in Finnish law.

The judgment will be read closely in other Baltic capitals that have recorded similar cable troubles. It shows that coastal states are willing to prosecute crew when evidence meets the criminal standard, not only to file diplomatic protests. Appeals or further detail on the ship's flag, owners and exact route may follow.

For shipping and telecom firms the message is practical: cable corridors are under tighter watch, and crews can face jail when a line is cut and prosecutors can prove aggravated damage. For the public the takeaway is simpler. An incident that once sat in the grey zone of suspected sabotage now has names, roles and prison terms attached by a Finnish court.
